power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.expanded: The CFA model including all predictors and fluency latent variables fit the data well, χ²(453) = 503.43, p = 0.05, CFI = 0.99, TLI = 0.99, RMSEA = 0.02 [90% CI: 0.00, 0.03], SRMR = .04.

table.header: Bivariate Associations Between Grade 2 Fall Predictors and Fluency
table.expanded: In contrast, discrete naming of digits and discrete naming of objects showed weak and declining associations (digits: ψ = .17-.39; objects: ψ = 0.05-0.21) with the association of discrete naming of objects not reaching significance at Grade 6 (ψ = .05, p = .529).

The full regression model including all Grade 2 predictors and autoregressive paths among reading fluency factors fit the data well, χ²(454) = 506.34, p = 0.045, CFI = 0.99, TLI = 0.99, RMSEA = 0.02 [90% CI: .004, .030], SRMR = .036.

However, because serial naming of digits emerged as a significant predictor (β = 0.358, p = 0.004) after removing serial naming of objects, suggesting shared variance between the two, we needed to verify which of the two is the best longitudinal predictor in the context of the other variables.

Discrete naming of words was then considered for removal but although it did not independently predict Grade 6 word reading fluency (β = -0.008, p = 0.951), its removal from the model destabilized the contribution of orthographic choice (β dropped from 0.30 to 0.26) and reduced R² for Grade 6 word reading fluency by 3% 1 As our focus is on the prediction of Grade 6 word reading fluency, and to avoid any distortions due to unmodeled paths, in every model through the trimming process, variables that are included as predictors of Grade 6 word reading fluency are also retained as predictors of Grade 2 and Grade 3 word reading fluency, regardless of their significance.

The resulting model, which only included variables contributing to the prediction of Grade 6 word reading fluency, is referred to as the "trimmed" model below, exhibiting good fit: χ²(144) = 201.97, p = 0.001, CFI = 0.99, TLI = 0.98, RMSEA = 0.04 [90% CI: .025, .051], SRMR = 0.04.2 We take this to be the most parsimonious model predicting Grade 6 word reading fluency.

This "comparison" model showed good fit to the data, χ²(476) = 529.78, p = 0.044, CFI = 0.99, TLI = 0.99, RMSEA = 0.02 [90% CI: .004, .030], SRMR = 0.04, and did not differ significantly from the full model, Δχ²(22) = 23.44, p = 0.38.

table.header: Suppressor Effects in the Longitudinal Prediction of Grade 6 Fluency

text.text: Purpose: Word reading fluency continues to develop after accuracy is achieved, yet which early skills drive this development beyond earlier attainment remains unclear.

We examined the longitudinal development of word reading fluency in Greek from Grade 2 to 6 to find out (1) how stable fluency is across these grades, (2) which early cognitive and linguistic skills predict Grade 6 fluency beyond prior attainment, and (3) whether the suppression effects commonly reported in concurrent designs hold longitudinally.

Greek children (n = 268) were assessed at the beginning of Grade 2 on serial and discrete naming (digits, objects, words, pseudowords), phonological awareness, orthographic knowledge, articulation rate, morphological awareness, vocabulary, and nonverbal ability, and on word reading fluency at the end of Grades 2, 3, and 6.
Longitudinal structural equation models with autoregressive paths were used to identify unique predictors.
Results: Fluency was highly stable (β = .88 from Grade 2 to 3; β = .64 from Grade 3 to 6).
Grade 2 fluency was predicted mainly by discrete word naming.

Beyond Grade 3 fluency, serial digit naming, orthographic knowledge, and articulation rate predicted Grade 6 fluency, accounting for an additional 13% of the variance, but only when discrete digit naming was included as a suppressor.
General cognitive and linguistic measures made no contribution.
The predictors of word reading fluency appear to change across the primary school years, from word-level naming to sequential processing, orthographic knowledge, and articulatory speed.
Word reading fluency may thus be better understood not as a unitary skill that simply improves quantitatively over time, but as a developmentally shifting construct.

Although word recognition accuracy is typically achieved within the first years of formal schooling in transparent orthographies (e.g., Altani et al., 2019; Landerl & Wimmer, 2008; Lerkkanen et al., 2004; Soodla et al., 2015), reading fluency continues to develop well into the later primary school years (e.g., Georgiou et al., 2014 Georgiou et al., , 2021;; Tobia & Marzocchi, 2014; Vaessen & Blomert, 2010).

text.text: What drives this continued development beyond early attainment, however, is not fully understood.

The present study examines the longitudinal prediction of word reading fluency from early Grade 2 to Grade 6 in Greek, using a multivariate longitudinal model that includes a broad set of cognitive and linguistic skills.
Reading fluency is widely regarded as a defining marker of skilled reading and stands among the core educational priorities of elementary education (National Reading Panel, 2000).
text.formatted: Reading fluency is widely regarded as a defining marker of skilled reading and stands among the core educational priorities of elementary education <ref type="bibr">(National Reading Panel, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Despite its central importance, reading fluency has been defined and operationalized in different ways, with definitions ranging from the rate of word decoding (Breznitz, 2006) to the joint product of accuracy, automaticity, and prosody that together support comprehension (Kuhn et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Despite its central importance, reading fluency has been defined and operationalized in different ways, with definitions ranging from the rate of word decoding <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Breznitz, 2006)</ref> to the joint product of accuracy, automaticity, and prosody that together support comprehension <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Kuhn et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: A key distinction concerns whether fluency is assessed through oral reading of connected text (text reading fluency, often termed oral reading fluency; e.g., Good & Kaminski, 2002) or through the rapid reading of lists of unconnected and unrelated words (word reading efficiency; as in the Test of Word Reading Efficiency; Torgesen et al., 1999).
text.formatted: A key distinction concerns whether fluency is assessed through oral reading of connected text (text reading fluency, often termed oral reading fluency; e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Good & Kaminski, 2002)</ref> or through the rapid reading of lists of unconnected and unrelated words (word reading efficiency; as in the Test of Word Reading Efficiency; <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">Torgesen et al., 1999)</ref>.

text.text: Although these two formats are often regarded as essentially identical at a surface level (e.g., Fuchs et al., 2001; Hudson et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2012) and are sometimes treated as interchangeable indices of the same underlying skill, they differ in an important respect: Oral reading fluency is confounded with comprehension and other supralexical processes such as syntactic parsing and semantic integration, which are engaged when reading connected text but not for word lists (e.g., Eason et al., 2013; Jenkins et al., 2003; Kim, 2015).

text.text: As a result, oral reading fluency performance may reflect a blend of word-level decoding efficiency and text-level comprehension skills, making it difficult to isolate the contribution of decoding efficiency.

Word reading efficiency, by contrast, offers a purer index of word-level processing efficiency, relatively free from the influence of text-level skills, and may therefore provide a more direct window onto the cognitive and linguistic skills underlying decoding efficiency (Protopapas et al., 2018).

text.text: For this reason, the present study focuses on word reading efficiency rather than oral (i.e., passage) reading fluency as the target of longitudinal prediction.
The ability to read individual words both accurately and rapidly is considered central to the development of reading fluency (e.g., Ehri, 2005; Hudson et al., 2009; Kim, 2015; Stanovich, 1980).
text.formatted: The ability to read individual words both accurately and rapidly is considered central to the development of reading fluency (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Ehri, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Hudson et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Kim, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">Stanovich, 1980</ref>).

text.text: Yet accuracy and speed do not emerge simultaneously or develop at the same rate.

As children develop as readers, individual differences in word reading shift from the accuracy dimension to the speed dimension, with this transition occurring once a minimum level of word reading accuracy has been established (Altani et al., 2020; Juul et al., 2014; Karageorgos et al., 2020).

text.text: In transparent orthographies, where decoding accuracy is typically mastered early, this shift occurs relatively quickly, such that large individual differences in reading ability come to be expressed primarily in speed well before the end of primary school (Eklund et al., 2015; Landerl & Wimmer, 2008; Mouzaki & Sideridis, 2007).

text.text: Despite this developmental progression, reading fluency shows strong autoregressive stability over time across orthographies (Georgiou et al., 2021; Khanolainen et al., 2020; Salins et al., 2026; van Viersen et al., 2018; Wei et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Despite this developmental progression, reading fluency shows strong autoregressive stability over time across orthographies <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Georgiou et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Khanolainen et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">Salins et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b103">van Viersen et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b105">Wei et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: However, this stability is imperfect and there is evidence for systematic variation in developmental trajectories.

Specifically, in addition to the stable trajectory, cumulative (Stanovich, 1986), compensatory (Baumert et al., 2012; Catts et al., 2012; Psyridou et al., 2020; Torppa et al., 2015), and late-emerging (Catts et al., 2012; Etmanskie et al., 2016; Leach et al., 2003; Psyridou et al., 2020; Torppa et al., 2015) trajectories have been documented, in which further fluency development is not fully accounted for by earlier fluency performance.
text.formatted: Specifically, in addition to the stable trajectory, cumulative <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">(Stanovich, 1986)</ref>, compensatory <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Baumert et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Catts et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Psyridou et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">Torppa et al., 2015)</ref>, and late-emerging <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Catts et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Etmanskie et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Leach et al., 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Psyridou et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">Torppa et al., 2015)</ref> trajectories have been documented, in which further fluency development is not fully accounted for by earlier fluency performance.

text.text: These trajectories have also been linked to different early cognitive profiles.

For example, longitudinal evidence from Finnish (a highly transparent orthography) suggests that persistent difficulties were associated with broad weaknesses in phonological awareness, rapid naming, and letter knowledge, whereas lateemerging difficulties were most clearly marked by slow rapid naming, and resolving difficulties by weaknesses confined to the preschool years (Torppa et al., 2015).

text.text: One possibility is that stability reflects trait-like continuity in a single homogeneous construct where a stable underlying ability drives performance throughout the developmental trajectory.
In this scenario, deviating patterns would be accounted for by extenuating factors disrupting an otherwise set progression.

Alternatively, the superficial long-term stability that is typically observed may belie a dynamic developmental process in which the cognitive and linguistic underpinnings of fluency shift across grades.

In this scenario, both the apparently stable and the deviating patterns could be attributed to the same processes, leading to convergent or divergent outcomes as a result of their developmental interlocking.
Addressing this question requires longitudinal designs that simultaneously track multiple cognitive and linguistic predictors to identify unique contributors to fluency development across grades.
Here, we take a first step toward this long-term goal by asking what early skills predict reading fluency development beyond prior attainment.

Serial naming (commonly termed "rapid automatized naming" or RAN) is among the most robust concurrent predictors of reading fluency across orthographies and developmental stages (e.g., Georgiou et al., 2016a,b; Moll et al., 2014, see also Araújo et al., 2015 for a meta-analysis).
text.formatted: Serial naming (commonly termed "rapid automatized naming" or RAN) is among the most robust concurrent predictors of reading fluency across orthographies and developmental stages (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Georgiou et al., 2016a,b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Moll et al., 2014</ref>, see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Araújo et al., 2015</ref> for a meta-analysis).

text.text: It is also a robust longitudinal predictor of reading fluency measures across orthographies, even when measured prior to reading instruction (although fewer studies have investigated the longitudinal relations and most findings have only examined a limited developmental range; e.g., Georgiou et al., 2012; Landerl et al., 2019; Lervåg & Hulme, 2009; McWeeny et al., 2022; Pan et al., 2011).
text.formatted: It is also a robust longitudinal predictor of reading fluency measures across orthographies, even when measured prior to reading instruction (although fewer studies have investigated the longitudinal relations and most findings have only examined a limited developmental range; e.g., <ref type="bibr">Georgiou et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Landerl et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Lervåg & Hulme, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">McWeeny et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Pan et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: This is important from a theoretical perspective because the cognitive processes underlying performance in reading fluency tests may change drastically during development.

Although one can always administer a passage or word list and obtain a superficially comparable metric of correct words per minute at any age, this does not mean that the task is performed in a comparable manner.
Children in early grades are likely to read many words by piecewise phonological recoding, whereas this is decreasingly likely at higher grades.

Moreover, children in early grades are likely to focus all their processing resources on one word at a time, essentially reading one word after the previous one has been completed, whereas children in higher grades are likely to overlap their processing across multiple successive words as they achieve actual fluency (Protopapas et al., 2013 (Protopapas et al., , 2018 (Protopapas et al., , 2024)), eventually reading as fast as they can speak rather than as fast as they can decode.

text.text: If the processes dominating test performance change during development, this means that different skill domains will dominate individual differences in reading fluency measures in different grades.

For this reason, different kinds of predictors may be longitudinally associated with reading fluency performance at different stages in reading development, and findings from early development (such as early predictors of Grade 2 reading fluency) cannot be generalized to later development (in late elementary or higher grades).

In this context, it is remarkable that serial naming has been found to be a strong and unique longitudinal predictor of reading fluency measures, beyond earlier attainment, both in early (from preschool to Grade 3, controlling for Grade 1; Diamanti et al., 2024) and later (Grade 2 to Grade 5; Romero et al., 2024) grades, in different orthographies (Norwegian and English, respectively).
text.formatted: In this context, it is remarkable that serial naming has been found to be a strong and unique longitudinal predictor of reading fluency measures, beyond earlier attainment, both in early (from preschool to Grade 3, controlling for Grade 1; <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Diamanti et al., 2024)</ref> and later (Grade 2 to Grade 5; <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Romero et al., 2024)</ref> grades, in different orthographies (Norwegian and English, respectively).

text.text: When considering naming tasks as predictors of reading fluency, a key theoretical distinction concerns whether naming is assessed in a serial format, where multiple stimuli are displayed simultaneously and named as quickly as possible from left to right, or in a discrete format, where stimuli are presented one at a time.

Serial naming has consistently been shown to be a stronger predictor of reading fluency than discrete naming across languages and grades (e.g., Altani et al., 2020; Logan et al., 2011; Protopapas et al., 2013), suggesting that processes specific to the serial format, beyond the speed of individual item retrieval, are critical for its relationship with reading.
text.formatted: Serial naming has consistently been shown to be a stronger predictor of reading fluency than discrete naming across languages and grades (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Altani et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Logan et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Protopapas et al., 2013)</ref>, suggesting that processes specific to the serial format, beyond the speed of individual item retrieval, are critical for its relationship with reading.

text.text: When both formats are included in the same model, discrete naming acts as a suppressor variable, removing shared item-level retrieval variance and thereby sharpening the unique contribution of serial naming to reading prediction (Logan et al., 2011; Logan & Schatschneider, 2014; Protopapas et al., 2013; van Viersen et al., 2024).
text.formatted: When both formats are included in the same model, discrete naming acts as a suppressor variable, removing shared item-level retrieval variance and thereby sharpening the unique contribution of serial naming to reading prediction <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Logan et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Logan & Schatschneider, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Protopapas et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr">van Viersen et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This suppression effect reveals a specific sequential processing component of serial naming that is not shared with discrete naming.

It has been proposed that this component concerns the ability to overlap processing stages across multiple successive items beyond single word recognition, referred to as cascaded processing (Protopapas et al., 2018).
text.formatted: It has been proposed that this component concerns the ability to overlap processing stages across multiple successive items beyond single word recognition, referred to as cascaded processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">(Protopapas et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Critically, however, this suppression effect has to date been demonstrated only in concurrent designs.

Whether it extends to longitudinal prediction, and whether the sequential component of serial naming carries a lasting influence on fluency development beyond early attainment, has not yet been examined.

Establishing the unique longitudinal contributions of serial and discrete naming therefore requires a multivariate model that simultaneously accounts for other cognitive and linguistic predictors of fluency.

Beyond naming speed, two additional predictors are examined here whose longitudinal contributions to reading fluency have received relatively little attention: orthographic knowledge and articulation rate.

Orthographic knowledge has been found to contribute significantly to efficient word reading across elementary grades, after controlling for reading skills, at least in transparent orthographies (Georgiou et al., 2012; Giazitzidou et al., 2025; Rothe et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Orthographic knowledge has been found to contribute significantly to efficient word reading across elementary grades, after controlling for reading skills, at least in transparent orthographies <ref type="bibr">(Georgiou et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Giazitzidou et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Rothe et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: It can be assessed with an orthographic choice task, which requires children to identify the correctly spelled word from a pair of phonologically identical alternatives.

Some researchers have suggested that this task measures word recognition rather than a distinct orthographic process, as readers who make correct orthographic choices probably have highly specified orthographic representations for those words, formed through orthographic learning (Nation & Castles, 2017).
text.formatted: Some researchers have suggested that this task measures word recognition rather than a distinct orthographic process, as readers who make correct orthographic choices probably have highly specified orthographic representations for those words, formed through orthographic learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Nation & Castles, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: However, evidence suggests that orthographic choice performance is not fully determined by the ability to read words in isolation and that it captures not only item-specific orthographic representations but also more general sensitivity to the patterns and regularities of the writing system (Compton et al., 2020).
text.formatted: However, evidence suggests that orthographic choice performance is not fully determined by the ability to read words in isolation and that it captures not only item-specific orthographic representations but also more general sensitivity to the patterns and regularities of the writing system <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Compton et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Whether this sensitivity carries unique longitudinal predictive value for word reading fluency beyond prior attainment and naming speed remains to be examined.
Articulation rate, on the other hand, is typically assessed by asking children to repeat sequences of words as rapidly as possible.

Since word reading efficiency involves overt articulation, articulation constraints may influence reading efficiency measures, so its inclusion allows its contribution to be properly separated from that of other predictors.
Two prior studies have found articulation rate to be a non significant predictor of reading development (Georgiou et al., 2021; Parrila et al., 2004).
text.formatted: Two prior studies have found articulation rate to be a non significant predictor of reading development <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Georgiou et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Parrila et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: However, these studies did not include discrete naming as a suppressor variable, leaving open the possibility that shared variance with naming speed may have obscured any unique contribution of articulatory efficiency to fluency development.
A broader set of cognitive and linguistic skills is also examined here within the same longitudinal framework.

In the early phases of reading development, phonological skills seem to be particularly important (e.g., Georgiou et al., 2008; Puolakanaho et al., 2007); however, as decoding becomes automatized in later grades, their unique contribution to fluency prediction diminishes, especially in more transparent orthographies like Greek (e.g., Georgiou et al., 2008; Landerl et al., 2019).

text.text: Alongside phonological skills, morphological awareness, a multidimensional component of the linguistic system that shares common variance with phonological and syntactic awareness (Levesque et al., 2021), has been proposed to influence literacy skills through multiple pathways.

text.text: However, evidence for a direct contribution of morphological awareness to word reading fluency is mixed.

In Greek, longitudinal studies have generally found no unique contribution once other predictors are controlled: Morphological awareness assessed in kindergarten and Grade 1 did not predict Grade 1 or Grade 2 word reading fluency after controlling for vocabulary and naming speed (Diamanti et al., 2017; Manolitsis et al., 2017), nor did morphological awareness at the start of Grade 2 predict fluency at the end of Grade 2 beyond phonological awareness and naming speed (Desrochers et al., 2018).

text.text: Finally, general cognitive skills (receptive vocabulary and nonverbal reasoning) are also added as control variables to ensure the specificity of the findings.

Examining all these skills within a single longitudinal model provides a more comprehensive picture of the early cognitive and linguistic predictors of word reading fluency across the primary school years and allows their respective contributions to be properly evaluated.
The present study examined the longitudinal prediction of word reading fluency in
Greek from Grade 2 to Grade 6.

Using a longitudinal structural equation modeling approach, we aimed to examine: (1) to what extent word reading fluency is stable from Grade 2 to Grade 6, (2) which early skills (assessed in Grade 2) uniquely predict later word reading fluency after accounting for prior attainment, and (3) whether the suppression effect of discrete digit naming on serial digit naming, previously reported in concurrent designs across languages, extends to longitudinal prediction.
Greek is a relatively transparent orthography in which grapheme-phoneme correspondences are largely consistent (Protopapas & Vlahou, 2009).
text.formatted: Greek is a relatively transparent orthography in which grapheme-phoneme correspondences are largely consistent <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Protopapas & Vlahou, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Although children typically achieve high levels of decoding accuracy early in reading development, substantial individual differences remain in the rate and efficiency with which words are processed (Protopapas, 2017).
text.formatted: Although children typically achieve high levels of decoding accuracy early in reading development, substantial individual differences remain in the rate and efficiency with which words are processed <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Protopapas, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Understanding which early skills contribute to later fluency is therefore important for clarifying the mechanisms underlying the development of reading efficiency in transparent orthographies.
To address this issue, the present study examined a broad set of cognitive-linguistic skills assessed at the beginning of Grade 2 as potential predictors of later fluency.

These included receptive vocabulary, nonverbal reasoning, phoneme awareness, syllable and phoneme blending, morphological awareness, orthographic knowledge, articulation rate, serial naming of digits and objects, and discrete naming of digits, objects, words, and pseudowords.

By examining multiple naming formats alongside linguistic and cognitive predictors within a single longitudinal model, the study aimed to clarify which early skills uniquely contribute to the development of word reading fluency over time.

Based on the results from previous longitudinal studies in transparent orthographies (e.g., Eklund et al., 2018; Georgiou et al., 2014 Georgiou et al., , 2021;; Khanolainen et al., 2020; Landerl & Wimmer, 2008; Psyridou et al., 2025), we expected word reading fluency to show high stability across the primary school years, even after accounting for measurement error, yet remain further predictable by early cognitive and linguistic skills beyond prior attainment.

text.text: Prior research suggests that the cognitive skills driving reading fluency may shift across development; phonological skills and letter knowledge are particularly important in the early phases of reading acquisition (e.g., Georgiou et al., 2008; Puolakanaho et al., 2007), while later fluency comes to be predicted increasingly by naming speed as decoding becomes automatized (e.g., Eklund et al., 2018; Torppa et al., 2012; van Bergen et al., 2014).

text.text: Thus, we expected the skills that uniquely predict fluency to differ between Grade 2 and Grade 6.

Finally, based on concurrent evidence across languages showing that discrete digit naming suppresses the contribution of serial digit naming to reading fluency (e.g., Logan et al., 2011; Logan & Schatschneider, 2014; Protopapas et al., 2013), we expected a similar suppression structure to operate longitudinally, isolating the sequential processing component of serial naming as a specific and lasting predictor of fluency development.

text.text: The sample comprised 268 students from 17 public elementary schools from a socioeconomically diverse sample of neighborhoods in the Athens metropolitan area.
All participants were native speakers of Greek.
Written informed consent was obtained from parents or guardians prior to participation.

The study received ethics approval from the ethics board of University of Alberta, Canada (study ID Pro00065133), and the directorate of primary and secondary education of the Greek Ministry of Education (Φ15/85312/91827/Δ1).
In accordance with Greek law, the permission to conduct the study in the public schools was renewed annually.
Participants were assessed across four waves: at the very beginning (fall) of Grade 2 in   2017, spring of Grade 2 (2018), Grade 3 (2019), and Grade 6 (2021 -2022).

text.text: Latent factors were constructed for all variables.
Word reading fluency was assessed with one task per time point (end of Grade 2, Grade 3, and Grade 6).

To account for measurement error, we specified dummy latent variables with a single indicator each, with residual variances fixed based on an assumed reliability of 0.94 based on prior data (Protopapas et al., 2007).

text.text: Error variance was then specified as (1 -reliability) × observed variance at each wave, yielding fixed (unstandardized) residuals of 0.002, 0.003, and 0.003 for Grades 2, 3, and 6, respectively.
To match the scale of the naming variables, fluency scores were also expressed as items per second (dividing raw scores by 60).

All predictors (receptive vocabulary, nonverbal reasoning, morphological awareness, phoneme awareness, syllable and phoneme blending, orthographic knowledge, articulation rate, discrete naming of words, pseudowords, objects, and digits, and serial naming of objects and digits) were also modeled as latent variables.
Most constructs were represented using odd-even split parcels as indicators, with loadings constrained to be equal across the two parcels of each construct.

Specifically, this applied to receptive vocabulary, nonverbal reasoning, phoneme awareness (combining phoneme deletion for words and pseudowords), syllable and phoneme blending, orthographic knowledge, and all four discrete rapid naming tasks.
Morphological awareness was represented by three observed subtask scores (analogy for words, analogy for sentences, derivation).
Articulation rate was represented by the five inverse-time scores (one per triplet).

Serial naming of digits and serial naming of objects were each represented by two indicators corresponding to fall and spring of Grade 2, with loadings across the two time points constrained to be equal.
Latent variances for all predictor constructs were fixed to 1.

Additionally, the residual covariances between the two phoneme deletion parcel indicators, and between Grade 2 spring serial digit and serial object duration scores, were freed to be estimated, to accommodate shared indicator-specific variance.
To examine the longitudinal development of word reading fluency, we first estimated a simple autoregressive model with paths from Grade 2 to Grade 3 and from Grade 3 to Grade 6 fluency.
This model served as the baseline for evaluating the incremental prediction of Grade 2 predictors over and above prior fluency attainment.

Next, to evaluate the bivariate associations between each Grade 2 predictor and reading fluency across time, we estimated a confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) model in which all predictor-fluency associations were specified as nondirectional covariances.
This model provided measurement-error-corrected latent correlations between Grade 2 predictors and reading fluency at each time point.

To determine which Grade 2 skills uniquely predicted Grade 6 reading fluency beyond autoregressive stability, we first estimated a multivariate structural model in which fluency at Grades 2, 3, and 6 was simultaneously regressed onto all predictors, while retaining the autoregressive paths.
To identify a parsimonious set of longitudinal predictors, we proceeded through a structured model-trimming sequence.
We first established the maximum proportion of variance in Grade 6 fluency that could be explained by all predictors simultaneously (the full model).
Then predictors that made negligible contributions to Grade 6 fluency were removed sequentially while monitoring changes in R² at each step.
Predictors were removed when their coefficients at Grade 6 were non-significant and their removal resulted in negligible changes in R².
Conceptually related predictors were evaluated in groups where appropriate.
The final trimmed (parsimonious) model was compared to the full model using a chi-square difference test.
The trimming sequence suggested potential suppression effects for some Grade 2 predictors, specifically for phoneme deletion, discrete digits, and discrete words.

To examine the nature and magnitude of these effects, we fit a series of supplementary models in which suspected suppressors were removed from the Grade 6 regression equation individually and in combination, while substantive predictors (serial naming of digits, orthographic knowledge, and articulation rate) were retained.
The primary focus of this analysis was on the Grade 6 outcome, given the aim of identifying longitudinal predictors beyond prior reading fluency skills.

Discrete word naming was treated separately from the other two suppressors because its role varied depending on model specification: It functioned as a significant predictor of early word reading fluency (Grades 2-3) but made no independent contribution to Grade 6 fluency, and its inclusion or exclusion affected the suppression dynamics of other predictors in Grade 6.

Model fit was evaluated using the chi-square value, the comparative fit index (CFI), the Tucker-Lewis index (TLI), the root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA), and the standardised root mean square residual (SRMR).
Good model fit was indicated by CFI and TLI ≥ 0.95, RMSEA ≤ 0.06, and SRMR ≤ 0.08 (Hu & Bentler, 1999).

text.text: Serial naming of digits and serial naming of objects showed strong associations with reading fluency across all waves (digits: ψ = .48-.60; objects: ψ = .41-.50).

In contrast, discrete naming of digits and discrete naming of objects showed weak and declining associations (digits: ψ = .17-.39; objects: ψ = 0.05-0.21) with the association of discrete naming of objects not reaching significance at Grade 6 (ψ = .05, p = .529).

The two discrete reading tasks, namely words and pseudowords, showed the strongest longitudinal associations with fluency across all time points, with discrete naming of words showing correlations ranging from .82 at Grade 2 to .52 at Grade 6.
Orthographic knowledge was also strongly associated with reading fluency across all waves (ψ = .46-.60).
Overall, all latent correlations (except for non-verbal reasoning) were attenuated from Grade 2 to Grade 6.

The full regression model including all Grade 2 predictors and autoregressive paths among reading fluency factors fit the data well, χ²(454) = 506.34, p = 0.045, CFI = 0.99, TLI = 0.99, RMSEA = 0.02 [90% CI: .004, .030], SRMR = .036.
This is referred to as the "full" model below.
The full set of predictors accounted for 80.4% of the variance in Grade 2 fluency, 80.5% in Grade 3 fluency, and 54.0% in Grade 6 fluency.
Grade 2 word reading fluency was significantly predicted by orthographic knowledge (β = 0.19), discrete naming of objects (β = -0.29), and discrete naming of words (β = 0.60).
Grade 3 word reading fluency was significantly predicted only by Grade 2 word reading fluency (β = 0.66).
Turning to the prediction of Grade 6 word reading fluency, after accounting for Grade 3 word reading fluency (β = 0.33), articulation rate (β = 0.21) emerged as the only significant predictor.

However, these results do not indicate which predictors are most useful in the model, because variables sharing most or all of their predictive variance with other variables will not appear as statistically significant even if the proportion of variance shared with the outcome is large.

For Grade 6 word reading fluency, four predictors remained significant over and above Grade 3 word reading fluency: serial naming of digits (β = 0.36), orthographic knowledge (β = 0.30), articulation rate (β = 0.19), and discrete naming of digits (β = -0.26).
Notably, the coefficients for discrete naming of digits and phoneme deletion (β = -0.09; ns) were negative.
As noted above, discrete naming of digits and, to a lesser extent, phoneme deletion, appeared to act as suppressor variables in the prediction of Grade 6 word reading fluency.
Therefore, a series of models were estimated, in which each suppressor was removed individually and in combination, to more directly probe their specific effects on the prediction of Grade 6 fluency.
To examine the role of discrete naming of words in the context of these potential suppressors, analyses were conducted both with and without discrete naming.

text.text: When both discrete naming of digits and phoneme deletion were removed from the Grade 6 model, all three substantive predictors (orthographic knowledge, articulation rate, serial naming of digits) became nonsignificant and R² for Grade 6 word reading fluency dropped from 0.532 to 0.466, a substantial reduction of 6.6%.
This suggests that the longitudinal predictive value of the three substantive predictors may depend critically on the presence of the suppressors.

Removing discrete naming of digits alone (retaining phoneme deletion) also resulted in a substantial deterioration: Grade 6 word reading fluency R² fell by 5.6% to 0.476, and serial naming of digits (β = 0.17, p = .08) and articulation rate (β = 0.15, p = .052) were no longer significant.

In contrast, removing phoneme deletion alone (retaining discrete naming of digits) led to a smaller reduction in explained variance: Grade 6 word reading fluency R² fell by approximately 1.0% to 0.523, and all three substantive predictors remained significant, although their coefficients were attenuated (orthographic knowledge: β = 0.23; articulation rate: β = 0.17; serial digit naming: β = 0.32).

The suppression effect of phoneme deletion was larger when discrete naming of words was also included as a predictor of early word reading fluency (1.0% drop) than when it was excluded from the model entirely (0.6% drop).
Finally, discrete word naming was examined as a substitute suppressor in the absence of discrete naming of digits and phoneme deletion.

In this case, predicted variance increased modestly (Grade 6 word reading fluency: R² = 0.481) compared to a model with no suppressors (R² = 0.454), and orthographic knowledge remained significant (β = 0.26, p = 0.035).
However, serial naming of digits and articulation rate did not recover significance, and R² remained approximately 5% lower than in the model including the two primary suppressors.
The present study examined the longitudinal stability of word reading fluency in Greek and the early cognitive and linguistic skills that uniquely predict fluency development from Grade 2 to Grade 6.

Fluency was highly stable across both transitions (Grade 2 to Grade 3: β = .88; Grade 3 to Grade 6: β = .64), indicating that earlier word reading fluency is the strongest single predictor of later word reading fluency.
Beyond the Grade 3 autoregressor, three early Grade 2 skills uniquely predicted Grade 6 word reading fluency: serial digit naming, orthographic knowledge, and articulation rate.

Their contributions depended on the presence of discrete naming as a suppressor: Serial digit naming and articulation rate were no longer significant without discrete digit naming, and orthographic knowledge without either discrete digit or discrete word naming.
Phoneme deletion acted as a weaker, secondary suppressor.
General cognitive and linguistic measures (nonverbal ability, vocabulary, morphological awareness, blending) made no contribution once fluency itself and the naming measures were in the model.
Of the three predictors, articulation rate emerged as the most robust as it remained significant across all model variants in which discrete naming was retained.
The results are consistent with autoregressive growth across Grades 2 to 6 with a constant standardized autoregressive path between successive grades of about .86 (as .86foot_0 ≈ .64).

Given that the reliability of this type of measure exceeds .9, this leads us to expect that at least 15% and up to 20% of word reading fluency variance in each grade is not attributable to previous fluency attainment but must be attributed to other systematic causal factors.

Prior research on the development of word reading fluency has indicated strong stability over time, with autoregressive coefficients ranging from 0.75 to 0.97 across Grades 1 to 9, depending on the study, grade level, and time interval (Khanolainen et al., 2020; Manolitsis et al., 2017; Salins et al., 2026; van Viersen et al., 2018), so the present estimates are in line with the literature.

text.text: However, despite this high mean-level stability, there is substantial variability in developmental word reading fluency trajectories at the individual level.
A proportion of systematic variance beyond the autoregressor is therefore to be expected.

Consistent with this expectation, the early Grade 2 predictors accounted for about 13% of Grade 6 variance beyond prior attainment at Grade 3, although we do not know how much of this would survive the statistical control of a Grade 5 autoregressor.

In addition, the early skills that uniquely accounted for this variance differed between Grade 2 and Grade 6: Discrete naming of words was the strongest predictor at Grade 2 but did not contribute to Grade 6 word reading fluency, where serial digit naming, orthographic knowledge, and articulation rate emerged as the main predictors.

Although much systematic Grade 6 variance is left to be accounted for by other factors, the fact that such a substantial proportion is attributable to long-term prediction from early skills strongly indicates that different skill domains contribute to word reading fluency growth at different developmental periods.
This also means that the well-established longitudinal stability of word reading fluency should not be conceived of as expression of a stable trait.
After all, a stable trait would lead to approximately equal pairwise correlations between any two grades, in stark contrast to the apparently autoregressive growth suggested by the present data.
Twin data are consistent with this picture.

Heritability of reading fluency is high and largely stable from age 7 to 16 (h2 = .73, .71, and .64), and the genetic influences at successive ages overlap substantially (rg = .84 from 7 to 12 and .78 from 12 to 16), with only small new genetic effects emerging at later grades (Tosto et al., 2017).

text.text: Most of the systematic variance at any age is therefore carried forward from earlier ages rather than newly arising.

If fluency at each grade builds on fluency at the previous grade together with the skills that are relevant at that stage, then the shift in predictors from Grade 2 to Grade 6 is the developmental counterpart of this statistical pattern.

This raises the possibility that, even where mean-level stability is high, word reading fluency itself undergoes qualitative change across development, with the same measure tapping partly different underlying processes in early and later grades, shifting toward more automatized processing as children progress through primary school.
Among the early skills examined, serial digit naming emerged as a robust unique predictor of fluency at both Grade 2 and Grade 6, with its contribution strengthening rather than weakening over time.

This finding is consistent with a substantial body of research showing that serial naming is a stronger correlate of reading than discrete naming across a range of languages and developmental stages (e.g., Altani et al., 2017; Georgiou et al., 2013; Logan et al., 2011; Protopapas et al., 2013; Vaessen & Blomert, 2010).

text.text: The serial format requires not only rapid retrieval of individual item names but also the efficient scheduling and coordination of multiple processes occurring simultaneously across a continuous sequence, demands that are absent in discrete naming where items are presented and named one at a time (e.g., Logan et al., 2011; Protopapas et al., 2013).

text.text: When both formats are included in the same model, discrete naming has been shown to act as a suppressor variable, removing shared item-level retrieval variance and thereby sharpening the unique contribution of the sequential component captured by serial naming (Logan et al., 2011; Logan & Schatschneider, 2014; Protopapas et al., 2013; extensively discussed by van Viersen et al., 2025).

text.text: Critically, this suppression effect has so far been demonstrated only in concurrent designs.
The present study extends this work by showing that the same suppression structure operates longitudinally in Greek and suggests that the effect may be even stronger longitudinally than concurrently.
Discrete digit naming assessed at the beginning of Grade 2 suppressed the association between serial digit naming and word reading fluency measured four and a half years later at Grade 6.
Removing discrete digit naming from the model resulted in a substantial drop in explained variance at Grade 6 (ΔR² = 5.6%), with serial digit naming no longer reaching significance.

This suggests that the sequential, coordinative component isolated by suppression is not merely a transient correlate of concurrent reading skill but reflects a more stable individual characteristic with a lasting influence on word reading fluency development.
One possible interpretation is that both serial and discrete digit naming involve familiarity with digit names and automatic access to their phonological forms.

However, serial naming additionally captures processes specific to the sequential nature of the task such as rapid eye movement control and the efficient scheduling of multiple items, that drive its relationship with reading (e.g., Georgiou et al., 2013; Gordon & Hoedemaker, 2016; Kuperman et al., 2016; Protopapas et al., 2024) beyond the automaticity of name retrieval (e.g., Stanovich et al., 1983; Logan et al., 2011).
text.formatted: However, serial naming additionally captures processes specific to the sequential nature of the task such as rapid eye movement control and the efficient scheduling of multiple items, that drive its relationship with reading (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Georgiou et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Gordon & Hoedemaker, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Kuperman et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Protopapas et al., 2024)</ref> beyond the automaticity of name retrieval (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">Stanovich et al., 1983;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Logan et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: By statistically controlling for the shared symbol naming component via discrete digit naming, the unique contribution of serial digit naming (i.e., the sequential processing component) to the longitudinal prediction of fluency is isolated and strengthened.

Moreover, the strengthening of the unique contribution of serial digit naming from Grade 2 to Grade 6 is consistent with the suggestion that word reading fluency undergoes qualitative change across development as children progress through primary school, moving beyond initial decoding toward more automatized word recognition and the efficient cascading thereby afforded (Protopapas et al., 2018 (Protopapas et al., , 2024)).

text.text: Both serial naming and word list reading share the demand of sustaining rapid, sequential responses across a continuous series of items.

As decoding becomes more automatized in later grades, the ability to efficiently maintain and coordinate this sequential processing may become increasingly critical for fluency, which may explain why the sequential component of serial naming, isolated through suppression by discrete naming, emerges as a stronger predictor of word reading fluency at Grade 6 than at Grade 2.

The predictive shift itself may be qualitative in nature, meaning that serial naming may predict word reading efficiency for partially different reasons at different stages of literacy development: indexing intraword processes early on and interword processes later on, as fluency develops (de Jong, 2011; Protopapas et al., 2013; van den Boer et al., 2026).

text.text: In sum, the consistent suppressive effect of discrete naming in the relationship between serial naming and reading, in both concurrent studies (previously) and the present longitudinal one, confirms that the prediction of reading fluency by serial naming is probably more about the "serial" than about the "naming" aspect of serial naming.

Whenever a pure naming measure (i.e., discrete naming) has been employed in conjunction with a RAN-type measure (i.e., serial naming) in an alphabetic orthography, a suppression effect has emerged, indicating that the relationship between RAN and reading cannot be primarily about whatever is shared with discrete naming.

This realization calls for a reconsideration of conceptualizing naming per se as a critical reading subskill and should perhaps moderate reference to naming deficits per se as potential contributing factors to reading difficulties.

Whereas the suppression effect of discrete digit naming operated on the sequential processing pathway, another suppression pattern emerged for orthographic knowledge, involving phoneme deletion awareness and discrete word naming as suppressors.

The suppression effect of phoneme deletion awareness alone was relatively modest (removing it while retaining discrete digit naming led to only a small reduction in explained variance at Grade 6 of approximately 1%, and orthographic knowledge remained significant, though attenuated).

However, the suppression effect of phoneme deletion was larger when discrete word naming was also present as a predictor of reading fluency than when it was excluded entirely, pointing to a three-way interplay among early phoneme deletion awareness, discrete word naming, and orthographic knowledge as predictors of long-term reading fluency.
One possible interpretation is that the longitudinal contribution of orthographic choice reflects sensitivity to the regularities and structure of the writing system.
Phoneme deletion and discrete word naming seem to capture phonological decoding variance that overlaps with orthographic knowledge but is not relevant for long-term fluency development.
When this shared variance is partialed out through suppression, the orthographic-specific contribution of orthographic knowledge becomes more apparent.

When discrete word naming was examined as a substitute suppressor in the absence of both primary suppressors (discrete naming of digits and phoneme deletion), orthographic knowledge remained significant but serial naming of digits and articulation rate did not recover significance.
This suggests that the suppression effect of discrete word naming operates primarily on the orthographic pathway rather than on the sequential processing or articulatory pathways.
This is consistent with the nature of the task, as discrete word naming is itself a word-reading task and therefore shares lexicalorthographic variance with orthographic knowledge.

This interpretation should be treated with caution, however, as the predictors were all measured at the same time point, so the suppression pattern reflects their shared variance rather than a directional relationship.
In the early phases of reading development, phonological decoding is effortful and relies heavily on phonological skills and letter knowledge (e.g., Georgiou et al., 2008; Georgiou et al., 2012).

This is consistent with concurrent evidence from Greek showing that orthographic knowledge contributes significantly to efficient word reading in both early and later primary school grades (Georgiou et al., 2012; Giazitzidou et al., 2025).

Moreover, measures of general orthographic knowledge, phonemic awareness, word frequency, and orthographic neighborhood size accounted for significant variance in orthographic choice performance beyond item-specific word reading skill.

This suggests that the orthographic choice task captures not only item-specific orthographic representations but also more general sensitivity to the patterns and regularities of the writing system, a component that is distinct from word reading.

The fact that it is not suggests that the general orthographic sensitivity component (beyond what is shared with word reading) is what carries the unique longitudinal predictive value.

The general orthographic sensitivity captured by our orthographic choice task may be indexing this dynamic capacity: Children with stronger sensitivity to orthographic patterns at Grade 2 may be more efficient orthographic learners going forward.

Consistent with this, studies on the self-teaching hypothesis (Share, 1995) have shown that prior orthographic knowledge (as measured using spelling choice tasks) significantly contributes to orthographic learning after controlling for decoding skills (Bosse et al., 2013; Cunningham, 2006; Cunningham et al., 2002; Nation et al., 2007).

Children who enter formal schooling with stronger general orthographic sensitivity may therefore continue to build richer and more precise word representations from subsequent reading experience, supporting this transition toward orthographic access and enabling faster and more fluent word recognition by Grade 6.
Beyond individual word representations, orthographic choice may also partly capture morpho-orthographic knowledge.

In Greek, many spelling distinctions are morphologically motivated (i.e., the correct spelling of a word ending often depends on its grammatical category or morphological structure; Protopapas et al., 2013).

text.text: Articulation rate emerged as a significant unique predictor of Grade 6 word reading fluency, remaining significant across all model variants in which discrete digit naming was retained.

This is a novel finding as, to our knowledge, no prior study has demonstrated a unique longitudinal contribution of articulation rate to word reading fluency beyond autoregressive stability and naming speed.

Indeed, most prior studies that have included articulation rate as a predictor have consistently found null results (Georgiou et al., 2021; Georgiou & Rothou, 2024; Parrila et al., 2004; but cf. Nikolopoulos et al., 2006).

In the present study, articulation rate was also non-significant in the absence of discrete digit naming; it is the suppressor effect of discrete digit naming (i.e., removing from both serial digit naming and articulation rate the variance they share with discrete digit naming, including the time taken to articulate each item) that reveals the unique longitudinal contribution of articulation rate.

This suggests that the predictive variance of articulation rate may have been obscured in prior studies by its shared variance with naming speed that was not absorbed by a discrete naming suppressor. (2021) reported that controlling for articulation rate was important in their study precisely because oral reading fluency involves articulation and their results showed that RAN's contribution to reading fluency remained significant and independent of articulation rate.

text.text: This is consistent with the view that serial naming and articulation rate tap partly overlapping but distinct processes: Serial naming captures sequential processing efficiency across a continuous array, while articulation rate captures the efficiency of articulatory execution.
Because discrete naming response times were measured to response offset, they include articulation time.
The suppression by discrete digit naming therefore removes not only shared naming speed variance but also the time needed to articulate a single item.
What remains in articulation rate after this may not be just articulatory speed.

It may instead reflect the flexibility of articulatory planning when multiple distinct articulatory patterns need to be produced in continuous succession, a demand shared with the speech rate task and list reading but is absent from discrete naming.
This component may constitute a specific constraint on reading fluency that becomes visible only at this level of model specification.
Fluent word list reading requires the rapid and sequential articulation of a series of items.
Children who can execute these articulatory sequences more efficiently may experience fewer bottlenecks in producing successive words, supporting faster and more fluent reading.
The fact that this effect emerges specifically at Grade 6 and not at Grade 2 is consistent with a developmental shift in the determinants of fluency.
In the early grades, when decoding is still effortful, articulatory efficiency may be less of a bottleneck as individual differences in fluency are more strongly driven by phonological decoding.

By Grade 6, as decoding becomes more automatized for most children, the speed at which words can be articulated in sequence may become an increasingly limiting factor for individual differences in fluency.

Thus, fluency tasks eventually become "articulation-limited" once readers are sufficiently skilled to read aloud as fast as they can articulate, evidenced by the lack of silent intervals in fluently read passages or serial word reading tasks (Protopapas et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Thus, fluency tasks eventually become "articulation-limited" once readers are sufficiently skilled to read aloud as fast as they can articulate, evidenced by the lack of silent intervals in fluently read passages or serial word reading tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Protopapas et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This pattern suggests that individual differences in articulatory speed may already have been present at Grade 2 but only became a relevant constraint on fluency once the decoding bottleneck was largely overcome.

Whether articulatory speed also becomes more stable as an individual difference across the primary school years, which would also provide a complementary explanation for the Grade 6 specificity of the effect, cannot be addressed with the present data, as articulation rate was measured only at Grade 2.
To our knowledge, no longitudinal studies have tracked the development of articulation rate across the primary school years, making it difficult to evaluate this possibility.

Future research examining its developmental trajectory alongside reading fluency would be needed to fully understand why articulatory speed emerges as a unique predictor only in the later primary school years and to establish whether the present finding replicates in other samples and orthographies.
Despite some strong findings with relatively clear potential interpretation, the present study is not without limitations.

Third, orthographic knowledge was assessed with a single word-level orthographic choice task.

Although the pattern of findings suggests that its longitudinal contribution reflects general sensitivity to the regularities of the writing system rather than item-specific orthographic representations, the present design cannot separate these two components, as both contribute to performance on every item.

Finally, although not a limitation of the design, the unique longitudinal contribution of articulation rate to Grade 6 word list reading fluency beyond prior attainment and naming speed is novel and, to our knowledge, has not been reported in prior longitudinal studies.
As such, it should be treated with caution until replicated in independent samples.
The present study examined the longitudinal prediction of word reading fluency in

Greek from the very beginning of Grade 2 all the way to Grade 6, using a longitudinal structural equation modeling approach that allowed the unique contributions of a broad set of early cognitive and linguistic skills to be examined simultaneously.

The results revealed high autoregressive stability in word reading fluency across the primary school years, even after accounting for measurement error, with early skills accounting for substantial variance beyond prior attainment.

Notably, the skills that uniquely contributed to this prediction differed between the early and later grades, from discrete word naming in the early grades to serial digit naming, orthographic knowledge, and articulation rate in the later grades.

This shift suggests that reading fluency in early and later primary school may be supported by partly different underlying processes, with word recognition moving from effortful phonological decoding toward more automatized processing subject to efficient cascading as children progress through primary school.

Critically, the unique contributions of these predictors were revealed through a suppressor structure involving discrete digit naming and phoneme deletion awareness, extending previously reported concurrent suppression effects to a longitudinal design and demonstrating that the sequential component of serial naming, as well as orthographic knowledge and articulatory speed, each carry specific and lasting influences on fluency development over and above prior attainment and naming speed.

These findings contribute to a growing body of evidence on the cognitive and linguistic foundations of reading fluency, and demonstrate that the unique longitudinal contributions of serial naming, orthographic knowledge, and articulation rate to fluency development are only fully revealed when suppressor variables are included in the model to purify their specific contribution, underscoring the value of examining competing predictor formats simultaneously within a single longitudinal framework.

Together, these methodological and substantive findings suggest that reading fluency is not a unitary skill that simply accumulates over time, but a developmentally shifting construct whose cognitive and linguistic underpinnings change across the primary school years.
